text.p: Washington Mutual Savings Bank said its proposed $6.5 billion merger with Great Western Financial Corp would produce 15 percent accretion to earnings in 1999.
The 1999 forecast is an upward revision from an initial estimate of 11 percent, a spokeswoman said, noting that pretax net interest income forecasts were also revised.

"We initially predicted $163 million in net interest income pretax for the combined company in 1999," the spokeswoman said. "That was revised to $246 million for 1999, which translates into 15 percent accretion," she said.
The information was disclosed Thursday in a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing regarding the merger.
The company also said it revised revenue enhancement projections to $334 million in 1999, from $251 million on a pretax basis, because of the increased forecast in net interest income.
Cost savings projections of $208 million in 1998 and $340 million in 1999 were unchanged.
Additionally, the spokeswoman said Washington Mutual executives would begin meeting with key investors next week to discuss the merger and to elaborate on the filing.
Great Western last week announced the merger agreement with Washington Mutual, moving to thwart a hostile bid by rival thrift H.F. Ahmanson and Co.
H.F. Ahmanson officials were not immediately available. The company on Monday said its bid was financially superior and more credible than Washington Mutual's offer.

Based on Thursday's stock prices, Ahmanson's offer to exchange 1.05 of its shares for each of Great Western's shares was valued at $42.40 a share, while Washington Mutual's offer to exchange 0.9 of a share for each of Great Western's was valued at $46.47 a share.

Sanford Bernstein analyst Jonathan Gray said he spoke with his clients Thursday and told them he believed Ahmanson's proposal was superior based on potential earnings power and its overlap with Great Western.
Gray said he did not believe Washington Mutual could accomplish the earnings it has projected. "I don't think they can earn what they're saying," Gray said.
The analyst also said he thought Ahmanson was likely to raise its exchange ratio to accomplish a merger.
